issue_context.title: /etc/vconsole.conf is overwritten by localectl without any comment, in contrast to the added comment at X onfig file
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

254.5-1

### Used distribution

arch

### Linux kernel version used

6.5.7

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

None

### Component

other

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

When localectl writes X config file, possibly by [x11_write_data](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/tree/v253/src/locale/localed-util.c#L470), it bothers to add a [comment who wrote it](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/tree/v253/src/locale/localed-util.c#L494-L496). I would expect a similar comment when it writes ``/etc/vconsole.conf`` by [vconsole_write_data](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/tree/v253/src/locale/localed-util.c#L415). One reason is so an unaware user would get a clue who overwrote his data.

It would be even better if any user comments that were in the ``/etc/vconsole.conf`` before it was overwritten would be preserved. Or that there would be a command line parameter ``--no-overwrite-config``. Users who prefer it that way might over write the files manually.
Edit: Instead, or in addition to, ``--no-overwrite-config``, ``--dry-run`` can do the trick. ``localectl --dry-run ...`` would do everything as before, except actually writing the files. Instead, it will print to ``stdout``, along with the filenames, what it would otherwise write to the files. The user can then decides what to do further.

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

/etc/vconsole.conf is overwritten with no comments what did it.

### Steps to reproduce the problem

1. ```su --login```
2. ```sed -i '1i\# a comment line' /etc/vconsole.conf```
3. ```localectl set-x11-keymap cz,us pc104 ,dvorak grp:win_space_toggle```
4. ```cat /etc/vconsole.conf```
Note no comment who rewrote the file, in contrast to the comment at X config.

### Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue

_No response_

review_comments:
here the comment `It's probably wise not to edit this file manually` makes a ton of sense, because we never read this file, we always overwrite it. vconsole.conf is the primary source of information after all, this xorg drop-in is only generated from it.

Hence, editing vconsole.conf manually is OK, but editing the xorg file is not, you will lose everything once localed rewrites anything.
